proxy_language: Old Welsh / Brittonic (Common Brittonic to Old Welsh stage) as a speculative proxy; 'Guoltintech' itself is not a securely attested language
proxy_rationale: 'Guoltintech' is not an attested language or ethnonym I can securely identify. The spelling with initial Guo- and final -tech/-tec resembles Old Welsh/Old Breton/Old Cornish orthography (guo- for later gwo-/gw-, -tec 'fair', Old Cornish/Breton tec, teg in Welsh), and 'guolt-' resembles Old Welsh guelt/gwallt 'hair' or guolt. The best defensible proxy is therefore Old Brittonic (Old Welsh c. 800-1100, Old Breton, Old Cornish) as a late court language of western Europe. The link is weak and based only on spelling; the current game names (Copod cila, Camari fusur, Hirgi, Tibep, Hidas, Kowu) show no Brittonic structure and should be replaced. If the studio intends a different language, this proxy should be revised.
phonology: Old Welsh/Brittonic consonants: stops p t c(k) b d g; fricatives f(v) th(/θ/) dd(/ð/) s ch(/x/) h; nasals m n; liquids l r (with voiceless rh, ll forms); semivowels w, i. Old orthography: c for /k/ everywhere, d for both /d/ and /ð/, t for /t/ and /θ/ (th appears), u for /v/ or /i/ in some positions, gu- for /gw/ (later gw-), uu for /w/. Vowels: a e i o u w y (Old Welsh y ~ /ɨ/ or /ə/), with long/short distinction; diphthongs ai au ei eu oe ou aw ew iw uw yw. Stress penultimate in Old Welsh and Old Cornish/Breton (final stress is a Breton/Cornish-specific shift not applicable to early forms).
phonotactics: Syllable (C)(C)V(C)(C); initial clusters limited (gw-, cr-, cl-, gr-, bl-, br-, tr-, dr-, pr-, pl-, cn-, gl-, sc-, st-, sp-). Word-final clusters like -nt, -lt, -rt, -nc, -rch, -nd, -ld, -st occur. No native word begins with ng, mb, nd as clusters in Old Welsh; voiceless stops and fricatives common in codas. Lenition (soft mutation) alters initial consonants after particles/in compounds (c>g, p>b, t>d, g>zero, b>f, d>dd, m>f, ll>l, rh>r). Native words almost never contain j, k, q, v, x, z in early orthography (v only as u).
orthography: Use conventional Old Welsh/Brittonic spelling in Latin letters: c not k; gu or gw for /gw/; u for /v/ medially; d/dd; ch /x/; th /θ/; ll, rh; vowels a e i o u w y; digraphs ae oe ei ou. Hyphens only in compounds if needed; apostrophes not used; no diacritics in the early forms (circumflex only optional in Modern Welsh for long vowels).
morphology: Highly inflectional historically but nominal case lost in Brittonic; two genders (masc/fem), plural by internal vowel change (affection) or suffixes (-ion, -oed, -ed, -on, -ydd, -au later). Adjectives follow nouns and agree with feminine nouns by soft mutation; verbs have personal endings. Common derivational suffixes: -ant, -wr (man), -ydd, -fa (place), -dre (home/town component), -in/-ig (diminutive), -og (having/full of), -wr agent, -edd/-ydd abstract; prefixes go- (under), ar-, di- (without), an-, cyf-/cy- (together), ym-, ad-, ail-, tra-.
compounding: Brittonic compounds are head-final in the older Celtic prefix-modifier pattern (e.g., modifier + head: cyf- + gwlad; pen- + dre), but the productive nominal phrase puts the modifying element after the head. Genitive relations are expressed by juxtaposition without an article: head + dependent (e.g., llys brenin 'court of a king', porth y mor 'port of the sea'). Place-names of the type 'fort/enclosure of X' use caer/din/dinas + personal name or feature; 'X-maker' formed with agent suffix -wr or element gwr/gof 'smith' (gof haearn). Compounds often lenite the second element (e.g., gwyn + tir > gwyndir), with linking vowel o/y/i frequently inserted.
noun_phrase_order: Noun + adjective (e.g., tir mawr 'great land'); noun + genitive noun (llys y brenin 'the king's court'); article y/yr/'r precedes noun; demonstratives and numerals precede or follow depending on word (numerals precede: tri gwr). Possessor follows possessed.

notes: The label 'Guoltintech' is not an attested language, so this entry is a speculative Old Brittonic (chiefly Old Welsh) proxy based only on the orthographic form (guo-, -tec). No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic; Brittonic is P-Celtic, so avoid Goidelic Q-forms (use p- where Goidelic has c-, e.g. pen not ceann). Replace the current game names, which show no Brittonic structure.
